replacement: Alyosha, as soon as he arrived, told Ivan that a little more than an hour before, Marya Kondratyevna had come running to his rooms with the news that Smerdyakov had killed himself. “I went in to clear away the samovar, and there he was, hanging from a nail in the wall.” Alyosha had asked whether she had told the police. She said she had told nobody, “but I flew straight to you, I ran the whole way.” She seemed to Alyosha completely out of her mind, and she was shaking like a leaf. He had run with her to the cottage and found Smerdyakov still hanging there. On the table was a note: “I destroy my life of my own will and desire, so as to put no blame on anyone.” Alyosha had left the note where it lay, gone straight to the police captain and told him the whole story. “And from him I’ve come straight to you,” Alyosha concluded, looking hard into Ivan’s face. All through his account he had kept his eyes on Ivan, as though something in his expression had startled him.

“Yes, but he’s spiteful. He laughed at me. He was insolent, Alyosha,” said Ivan, with a shudder of offense. “But he was unfair to me, unfair to me about lots of things. He told lies about me to my face. ‘Oh, you’re about to perform an act of heroic virtue: you’ll confess that you murdered your father, that the valet killed him at your instigation.’”

Some of the ladies, particularly those from out of town, showed up in the gallery very smartly dressed. But most of them had stopped thinking about clothes at all. Their faces showed a hysterical, intense, almost morbid curiosity. One odd fact, which many observations confirmed afterwards, was that nearly all the ladies, or at least the vast majority, were on Mitya’s side and wanted him acquitted. This was perhaps mainly because he was known as a conqueror of women’s hearts. People knew that two women who were rivals would take part in the case. One of them, Katerina Ivanovna, was the center of general interest. All kinds of extraordinary stories went around about her, amazing anecdotes about her passion for Mitya in spite of his crime. People especially stressed her pride and her “aristocratic connections” (she had visited hardly anyone in the town). They said she meant to ask the Government for permission to follow the criminal to Siberia and marry him somewhere in the mines. Grushenka’s appearance in court was awaited with just as much impatience. The public looked forward with anxious curiosity to the meeting of the two rivals, the proud aristocratic girl and “the hetaira.” But the ladies of the district knew Grushenka better than they knew Katerina Ivanovna. They had already seen “the woman who ruined Fyodor Pavlovitch and his unhappy son.” Almost every one of them wondered how father and son could be so in love with “such a very common, ordinary Russian girl, who wasn’t even pretty.”
